title: The king of the island
hookLine: tradition places Nanak at the court of Raja Shivnabh in the south, who waited years to meet him

lines: A TRADER STEPS OFF A BOAT.
WHO TAUGHT YOU TO LIVE LIKE THIS?
cards: A trader steps off a boat onto an island in the far south. On a day when the town keeps a fast, he doesn't. He gets up before dawn, sings, and then goes to work.
Word reaches the palace, and the king sends for him. Who taught you to live like this? The trader names a teacher far away in the north.
And the king, the story says, decides he will not rest until that teacher stands in his court.

teach.h: A SIKH TRADER ON THE ISLAND.
teach.b: The janamsakhis call him Raja Shivnabh, a king on an island in the south. The trader is remembered as Bhai Mansukh, a Sikh of Guru Nanak.

teach.h: THE KING WAITS, AND IMITATORS COME.
teach.b: Tradition says the king asked how he would know the Guru if he came, and Mansukh said, roughly, you'll know when your heart goes quiet. So the king waited. In the telling, for years.
And waiting made him a target. Word got out that the king longed for a holy man, and pretenders arrived, dressed for the part, full of fine speeches, hands out for gifts. The king received every one.

teach.h: A SINGER SITS IN A GARDEN.
teach.b: Then, the story goes, a traveler sat down quietly in a garden outside the city, with a companion and a rabab, and began to sing. No announcement.
The king tested him with dancers and gifts, to see whether this man too could be bought or flattered. Nanak was not moved.
And the king's heart, at last, went quiet. The story knows that real waiting doesn't settle for the nearest impressive person.
That a long wait draws imitations, and part of waiting well is telling the loud thing from the true one. That the real one came plainly, to a garden, not a throne.
And that one person living honestly on an island was the whole reason a king started looking.

how: Sikhs retell the sakhi of Raja Shivnabh as a story of longing and recognition, and gurdwaras connected with Guru Nanak's southern journey keep his memory.

games.q: you're the king. you've waited a long time for a teacher, and another impressive holy man arrives at court, asking for gifts. what do you do?
o: accept him; the wait has been long enough.
receive him, and keep waiting for the one who quiets your heart.
games.why: in the telling, Shivnabh received them all and kept waiting, until a singer in a garden turned out to be Nanak.

practice: Choose something you're waiting on right now, a reply, a result, a season of life to end, and name it once, quietly.
Then just wait, the way the king waited, with the door open, and when the urge to grab the nearest substitute comes, let it pass. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Raja Shivnabh, who in the story waited for Nanak, turned away every imitation, and knew the true one when his heart went quiet.

carryVoice: Your line: worth the wait. The true one came quietly, to a garden. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.
